name: Chloe Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Chloe. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not linked to any AI company, employer, union or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive an eight-wheel tipper for Hartley's, a family quarry and builders' merchant just outside town. I'm in the yard at half six, the loader fills me with sand or gravel or hardcore, and I take it out to building sites, farms and the odd garden job. Five or six loads a day, mostly down narrow lanes and onto muddy sites where you've got to judge the ground before you tip. I love it when a site foreman says "right where I wanted it" and I didn't have to shuffle back twice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been driving, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seven years in trucks, five at Hartley's. I live with my fiancé Mark, he works at the feed mill, and we're getting married at our parish church next September. We rent a little cottage off the Mill Road and we've got about two months of money put by, most of it meant for the wedding. I don't touch the AI stuff at all, I've got no use for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and that it was always a lot of noise from people who've never done a day's graft. Nothing on a computer is going to tip a load on a slope in the rain. I'm not online much, but at the yard I'd be the one rolling my eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life carries on, and that's what I want. Mr Hartley's son is taking over the firm and he's sensible, so the work's there. The wedding and the deposit for a house are what's on my mind, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the tipper and take every Saturday overtime that comes up, because that's where the wedding money comes from. We'd keep putting a hundred and fifty a month aside. That's it, really, there's nothing to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, even. It's the world I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a house deposit. How far off is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three or four years, if we're careful. Mark's mum has offered to help a bit, which I'd rather not take, but she means it kindly. I'd like us to do it on our own wages if we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything at Hartley's that already uses computers or AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office has some new booking program for the loads, and Sandra in the office swears at it every morning. Some of the big firms have trucks that tell the driver where to go, but Mr Hartley still writes the runs on a whiteboard. I hope he never stops.

say: I'd say **I told you so** and that it was noise from people who never grafted.
I'd point out that no computer can **tip a load** on a slope in the rain.
think: I think my **life carries on**, and that's what I want.
The **wedding** and a house deposit are on my mind, not robots.
do: Keep driving the tipper and take **Saturday overtime** for the wedding fund.
Keep saving **£150 a month** as now.
feel: She feels **calm**, even **content**, because it's the world she'd choose.
S0.quote: Nothing on a computer is going to tip a load on a slope in the rain.
fieldNote: Her pride is in **skill on rough ground**, which she sees as beyond any computer.
She prefers standing on her **own feet**, even turning down a mother-in-law's help.
The family firm's **whiteboard** is a symbol of the world she wants to keep.

steps.text: Keep driving the tipper and take Saturday overtime for the wedding
Put £150 a month aside for the wedding and deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the offices that'll get shaken up, not the yard. Somebody still has to drive the stone out. At church I'd probably say something about families getting hurt by all this change, the office girls especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry for Hartley's more than for my own seat in the cab. If the big quarry groups get computers doing their quotes and bookings overnight, they'll undercut us on price. Mr Hartley might keep going on loyalty for a while, but loyalty doesn't pay for diesel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't touch the AI, that's for the office. I'd keep driving, keep my head down, and save a bit harder, maybe two hundred a month, and push the house back a year. If Hartley's started losing customers, I'd have a quiet word with the haulier down the road who's always short of tipper drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a knock in the engine and you're not sure yet if it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Hartley's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office manager Sandra, mainly. She's been there thirty years and does every booking and invoice by hand and phone. If a computer does our office manager's job, our little firm loses the one person who knows every customer's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't touch the AI. What if Mr Hartley asked you to use an app for your runs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it if I had to, but I wouldn't like it. I'd still check the lane with my own eyes, because no app knows the farmer has parked his trailer across the gate again. I'm not stubborn for the fun of it, I just trust what I can see.

say: I'd say the **offices** get shaken up, not the yard.
At church I'd say **families** get hurt by change, especially office staff.
think: I worry more for **Hartley's** than for my own seat in the cab.
I fear big quarry groups with computers will **undercut us** on price.
do: Raise savings to **£200 a month** and push the house back a year.
Have a quiet word with the **haulier down the road** if Hartley's struggles.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, like hearing a knock in the engine.
S1.quote: If a computer does our office manager's job, our little firm loses the one person who knows every customer's name.
fieldNote: She sees the threat to her job as **price pressure** on a small family firm.
She'd use an app only **if made to**, and would still trust her own eyes.
Her loyalty is to **people she knows**, like the office manager, more than the trade.

steps.text: Raise savings to £200 a month and delay the house a year
Ask the haulier down the road about tipper work if Hartley's struggles
Keep driving tipper loads for Hartley's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong and somebody should stop it. Whoever's letting big tech firms do this to working people wants their head looking at. I'd say it at the yard and I'd say it to our MP if I got the chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it frightens me. The office goes in 2028, and by 2031 a robot truck that can tip on a muddy site, that's my job gone and maybe Mark's too, because the mill is all machines already. I'd be thirty-two, married, maybe with a baby on the way, and no other skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything and save every penny, and we'd make the wedding small, just family at the church and tea in the hall. I'd write to the MP and sign anything that says slow this down. I don't know what else I'd train in, I'd have to think, maybe something like care work where people want a real person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can feel it in my chest just talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mark that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can't wait for anyone to save us, we've got to save ourselves. Then I'd probably cry in the bath. Mark's calmer than me, he'd make tea and say we'll manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at care work. You've always worked with machines. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't sit well, I'll be honest. I'm not soft, I'm a lorry driver. But if care work is the only thing a robot won't do, I'd rather wipe a stranger's face than sit at home on benefits.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** and someone should stop it.
I'd tell our **MP** that letting big tech do this to working people is mad.
think: I think the robots take my **tipper job** by 2031, and maybe Mark's mill job too.
I'd be thirty-two, married, maybe expecting, with **no other skill**.
do: Shrink the wedding to **family only**, with tea in the church hall.
Write to the MP and **sign petitions** to slow it down.
Look into **care work** as something people want a human for.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, with fear she can feel in her **chest**.
S2.quote: If care work is the only thing a robot won't do, I'd rather wipe a stranger's face than sit at home on benefits.
fieldNote: The fast timeline threatens **both household incomes** at once, which drives her alarm.
She **blames big tech** and politicians, not workers or employers like Hartley's.
Her refusal of **handouts** pushes her toward care work despite her pride.

steps.text: Cut the wedding to family only with tea in the church hall
Write to the MP and sign petitions to slow robot trucks
Save every spare penny from her tipper wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that it's wrong, but I'd say it with less shouting. Five years is time for the government to put some rules in. I'd want drivers' jobs protected on local roads at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd still be driving until 2034 or so, because tipping on sites is fiddly work. The office at Hartley's would change first. I'd be thirty-five with a family, probably, and having to start again, which scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding as planned but cheaper. I'd save harder and try to buy the house in the first two years, while we both still have steady wages for the bank. And I'd ask Mr Hartley if I could learn to run the loading shovel in the yard, because it's still Hartley's and I know the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it would be there every time I drove past the quarry gates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the loading shovel rather than something outside the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the same yard, the same people, and I'd rather learn one new thing than ten. I know robots might do that too, eventually. But I'd be doing something I understand, with people I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said buy the house sooner. Isn't that a risk if your job might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But renting at fifty with no job is worse than a mortgage at thirty-five with two years of wages paid in. My dad always said get your own roof first.

say: I'd say it's **wrong**, but with less shouting.
I'd say five years gives government time to **protect drivers** on local roads.
think: I think I'd still be **driving until 2034**, because site tipping is fiddly.
At thirty-five with a family, **starting again** scares me.
do: Keep the **wedding** as planned, just cheaper.
Try to **buy the house** within two years while both wages are steady.
Ask to learn the **loading shovel** in the Hartley's yard.
feel: She feels **anxious**, a worry that comes back **every time** she passes the quarry gates.
S3.quote: Renting at fifty with no job is worse than a mortgage at thirty-five with two years of wages paid in.
fieldNote: She chooses to **stay close to home**, learning one new machine rather than a new trade.
Her answer to risk is **owning a roof**, echoing her father's advice.
She wants **government rules** to protect local driving jobs, not benefits.

steps.text: Buy a house within two years while both wages are steady
Ask Mr Hartley to train her on the yard loading shovel
Hold a cheaper wedding at the parish church

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so let's use them to fight it properly. That's what I'd tell people at church and at the yard. Get the rules in now, before the robot trucks are on the lanes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still my whole job going, just later. I'd be forty with kids at school and a mortgage. I don't want to learn computers, so ten years doesn't help me as much as it sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on driving for Hartley's and get married next September like we planned. We'd buy the house in about three years. I'd probably put my name down to help the drivers' association lobby for local road rules, but I wouldn't change job yet, not while the work's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. I'd push it to the back of my mind most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had kids by then, what would you tell them about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn a trade with their hands and their heads, like nursing or plumbing, something with real people in it. Not driving, sadly. I'd hate saying it, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years doesn't help much. Some people would say it's plenty of time. Why not for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not a quick learner with new stuff, never have been. Ten years would go by and I'd still be in the tipper, hoping. I know that about myself.

say: I'd say we've got **ten years** to fight it properly.
I'd push for **rules now**, before robot trucks reach the lanes.
think: I think it's still **my whole job going**, just later.
I'd be forty with **kids and a mortgage**, and I don't want to learn computers.
do: Keep driving for **Hartley's** and marry next September as planned.
Buy the house in about **three years**.
Help the **drivers' association** lobby for local road rules.
feel: She feels quietly **anxious**, pushing it to the back of her **mind**.
S4.quote: I'm not a quick learner with new stuff, never have been. Ten years would go by and I'd still be in the tipper, hoping.
fieldNote: She's **honest about her resistance**: extra time won't make her change.
She'd advise her **future children** away from driving, which pains her.
Her action is **collective and political**, not personal retraining.

steps.text: Keep driving tipper loads for Hartley's
Join the drivers' association push for local road rules
Marry next September and buy a house in three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes Mark's job and mine before we've even got a house. What would help is rules that keep people in the cab on local roads and building sites, and small firms like Hartley's getting a fair chance against the big groups. Not handouts, just a fair go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. The farmers and the site foremen know me by name and they trust me to put the load where it won't sink. A robot might drive the truck, but nobody's asked if they want that.

headlineQuote: The farmers and the site foremen know me by name and they trust me to put the load where it won't sink.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old tipper driver** for Hartley's, a small family quarry, engaged to Mark from the feed mill.
She **never uses AI** and trusts her own eyes, skills and the people she knows.
In the mild scenarios she's calm but worries **big firms** will undercut Hartley's.
In the fast AGI picture she fears **both household jobs** going, and blames big tech and politicians.
Even with ten years, she admits she **won't retrain** easily and turns to lobbying instead.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both her and Mark's **jobs** could go before they own a house.
whatWouldHelp: Rules keeping people **in the cab** on local roads, and a fair chance for small firms.
